scores.why: Power side-channel anomaly detection as an independent check on what device software reports, with alerts sent over a separate authenticated LoRa path. Rare at a hackathon, though power-based intrusion detection exists in research.
Fits 'detect earlier' and keeps working when IP networks are compromised or down: the LoRa link is treated as hostile, every frame is signed and encrypted, and replays are rejected.
Systemd installers, node enrollment and an operations runbook, but each monitored device needs its own current sensor and USB oscilloscope, and the detector is a simple CUSUM on mean voltage.
Polished landing page with an isometric solar-field illustration, a 75-second captioned film and a hand-built command-console dashboard.
The whole chain is in code (ESP32 firmware, acquisition, CUSUM voting, crypto protocol, SQLite, Flask API, dashboard); no tests and duplicated node code.

projects.live_demo: Landing page and film respond; the dashboard needs the hardware
strengths: Real end-to-end hardware pipeline with sound cryptography and replay protection
Alert channel independent of IP networks suits degraded conditions
Detailed README: threat model, math, deployment, runbook
weaknesses: Basic mean-shift detector, untested on real loads
Needs lab-grade sensor and oscilloscope per device
red_flags: The anomaly in the demo is self-induced by a keypad-triggered workload
Whole MVP landed in one overnight commit
projects.verdict: Strong, genuinely built defensive prototype that fits the brief; held back by a staged anomaly, simple detection and no tests.

scores.why: A pocket Tor gateway with its own LTE modem closely resembles existing Tor travel routers, and Orbot VPN mode covers much of the gain; docs admit the modem and SIM still identify the user.
Security for at-risk journalists fits 'prevent' loosely, but it is an individual privacy tool, not resilience or continuity, with no degraded-scenario demo.
The prototype carried phone traffic over LTE but logs show timeouts and low throughput; no Tor config or kill-switch in the repo; hardware is a Pi 4 dev setup far from the concept size.
Very polished deck, brand kit, CAD exploded views and Blender renders; dashboard not shown.
Real code is router NAT/DNS scripts, not Tor, plus a dashboard on simulated data; much of the repo is render, video and voiceover scripts.

strengths: Clear target users and a human-centred story
Strong presentation, branding and industrial-design concept
Honest status doc separating working from aspirational
Dashboard has an API contract and tests
weaknesses: Tor routing and the fail-closed kill-switch are not in the repo
Effort weighted toward marketing over product code
Weak novelty against existing Tor routers
red_flags: Deck shows a 'Tor Check' success while the repo's router config is plain NAT
projects.verdict: A well-presented privacy-gadget concept whose key security mechanism is shown only in video, and which loosely fits the resilience brief.

calibration_note: LayerOne lands in the strong-prototype band for real working hardware and crypto that fits the brief; SafeWall sits near a typical prototype because its polish outruns its implementation.
